title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost

paper.title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reasoning substantially improves language models’ ability to solve difficult
problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer
tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the
problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this
goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved.
We investigate whether open-weight models can generate less verbose reasoning
by changing the form of their own earlier thoughts, without retraining.
Our intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before
pending tool results are revealed, then compares continuations from original
and compact histories. Across the tested models, accepted compact histories
usually shorten future reasoning; a coding case study also shows less repeated
verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments,
compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive
time depend on the target and compressor. These findings identify reasoning
history as one way to reduce future reasoning-token use and motivate
model-specific compaction policies evaluated for both efficiency and retained
capability.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reasoning is a major source of language-model capability: generating intermediate steps improves problem solving, and recent reasoning models extend these gains to complex coding and tool use ( Wei et al., 2022 ; OpenAI, 2026a ) . Those gains carry a substantial inference cost. In Artificial Analysis data retrieved on August 3, 2026, reasoning accounts for 84.9% of generated tokens for GLM 5.2 and 75.1% for Claude Fable 5. For DeepSeek V4 Pro, reasoning output alone accounts for 53.4% of total API cost ( Artificial Analysis, 2026 ) . Reasoning can therefore dominate generated output, while agents also repeatedly pay to process earlier scratchpads as input history. The goal of efficient reasoning is to retain the analysis needed to solve a problem while reducing repeated analysis and low-value tokens. OpenAI reports that GPT-5.5 improves coding performance over GPT-5.4 while using fewer tokens ( OpenAI, 2026a ) . Practical inspiration for this study came from occasional, unofficial exposures of GPT-5.5’s reasoning scratchpad, which appeared compact (Appendix F ). These observations are anecdotal, and the scratchpads are not reliably accessible for controlled study: OpenAI does not officially expose raw reasoning ( OpenAI, 2026b ) . We therefore study open-weight models whose reasoning is accessible for observation and controlled rewriting. Open-weight models may already be capable of expressing useful reasoning compactly, even when their default responses are verbose. We test whether rewriting earlier scratchpads as concise state records can encourage these models to use less reasoning without new training. Prior reasoning may serve as an in-context example of how concisely to express subsequent analysis. Changing its form could therefore reduce newly generated reasoning, beyond the immediate saving from shortening the input. The rewrite is instructed to preserve decisions, uncertainty, and intended actions; the target receives no new instruction to be brief. Concise demonstrations and surrounding context already influence reasoning length ( Jin et al., 2024 ; Renze and Guven, 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Ge et al., 2025 ) . Reasoning Shift shows that added context can shorten reasoning and verification, sometimes at a quality cost ( Rodionov et al., 2026 ) . Related approaches manage agent context ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Lian et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) or steer concise reasoning states ( Azizi et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . We isolate a rewrite of the model’s own earlier reasoning while preserving other messages and withholding future tool results from the compressor. We first test whether this intervention changes subsequent generation in paired continuations, then evaluate continuous compaction in software agents. The controlled results show frequent shortening across model families, while deployment quality and economics vary by target and compressor. Compaction is thus a candidate route toward more efficient reasoning, with practical value that must be assessed per model rather than inferred from shorter traces alone. sections.heading: Reasoning-only compaction.
sections.text: A compressor LLM converts historical assistant scratchpads into shorter state records. It is instructed to retain decision-relevant facts, numbers, uncertainty, conclusions, and intended actions while removing repetition. System and user messages, tool calls, arguments, and observations remain intact. The target’s weights, tools, and current instructions are unchanged. We compare original ( clean ) and rewritten ( compact ) histories; Table 5 gives an example. Code and frozen experimental records for reproducing the analyses are released at https://github.com/DebelToni/ShortReasoning .

sections.heading: Outcome-blind timing.
sections.text: During shared acquisition, each rewrite completes after an action is requested and before its result is executed or revealed. At the fork, the histories are frozen and independently continued under the same model/provider route and settings (Figure 1 ). Serialized first requests are checked field by field to verify that only assistant reasoning differs. Consequently, the first-turn contrast measures the effect of the history intervention after a shared observation; later contrasts can also reflect treatment-induced trajectory changes.

sections.heading: Effect on subsequent reasoning.

A source history is one model’s partially completed run on one task. Precontinuation gates retain 58 of 72 model-specific source histories: five fail action checks and nine fail fidelity checks. Three paired continuations per accepted source yield 174 quality pairs and 172 comparable token pairs (Table 1 ). sections.heading: Turnwise and style patterns.
sections.text: Figure 3 (a) examines shortening across turns in the initial DeepSeek/Laguna comparison (72 pairs). Pooled token reductions grow from 8.8% on turn one to 56.1% on turn three; later turns can also reflect changes in previously generated text and actions. Panel (b) compares five history styles on ten DeepSeek sources, with three continuation blocks each. More compact styles have larger median reductions, although individual responses are not consistently ordered. This sweep uses sources with known outcomes and jointly varies length, syntax, wording, and compressor provenance, leaving the mechanism unresolved (Appendix C ).

sections.heading: Rewrite properties and length-matched controls.
sections.text: To test whether generic rewording elicits shorter continuations, we compare original histories with fresh paraphrases constrained to 90–110% of their word count. Across 65 comparable pairs, median future reasoning changes by + 0.7 % +0.7\% (95% CI [ − 8.2 , + 9.7 ] [-8.2,+9.7] ), while exact success falls from 68/69 to 59/69. The near-zero median change gives little evidence of systematic shortening from this paraphrase intervention. Its lower success rate leaves the specific contribution of history length unresolved.

sections.heading: Setup and accounting.
sections.text: We compare continuous compaction with normal history on a fixed 50-task SWE-bench Verified Mini sample ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) . Four targets use GPT 5.6 Luna as an external compressor or compact their own reasoning. Before each target request, new reasoning blocks are compacted and cached using only their text and action name. Blocks of at most 12 words stay unchanged; non-shorter rewrites revert to the original. We reanalyze existing captures while keeping the original evaluated run for every task, including unsolved runs and model-limit exits. The accounting links saved target responses and associated rewrites to the same run. Earlier abandoned attempts are excluded. Appendix D.5 defines this conditional accounting; Appendix D.6 explains excluded requests and accounting limits. Spend includes rewriting; the main table reports target time excluding rewriting. We sum client-observed request durations, including queueing and network transfer, but exclude tools, orchestration, and evaluation. These sums do not measure elapsed task time. Nemotron target usage uses a common tariff, with captured compressor charges. Provider changes remain part of these comparisons.

sections.heading: Results and practical interpretation.
sections.text: Six of eight compaction configurations cost less, and seven reduce target request time (Table 3 ). Only the two MiniMax configurations reduce rewrite-inclusive request time (Appendix D.5 ). Kimi self-compaction has a small inclusive time increase that rounds to zero. Rewriting can outweigh time saved on the target’s own requests. A self-compressor may generate substantial reasoning before it returns a short block. Table 4 reports an exploratory test of lower compressor effort. Observed success differs from Normal by at most three of 50 tasks. These results do not establish quality preservation. Paired task-bootstrap intervals in Appendix D.4 describe uncertainty over the assigned tasks while holding the captured runs fixed. Median times are confounded by provider and possible checkpoint differences (Appendix D.7 ). To understand differences in agent work, we retrospectively count tool calls in the selected terminal trajectories, excluding abandoned attempts. Changes range from − 29.8 % -29.8\% to + 19.8 % +19.8\% . Kimi with external compaction illustrates the combination of more steps and shorter reasoning: selected assistant responses rise from 1,842 to 2,304 ( + 25.1 % +25.1\% ), while mean reasoning per response falls 31.1% and total reasoning falls 13.8%. This arithmetic decomposition explains the total change through response frequency and reasoning length per response. Preprocessing amortization and single-task marginal latency are analyzed separately in Appendix E ; the hosted one-use example loses both time and money.

sections.heading: 4 Discussion
sections.text: Our controlled comparisons show that changing how earlier reasoning is written can reduce how much reasoning a model generates next. The target receives no new instruction to be brief. We still do not know which changes cause the shortening. Rewrites may remove repetition, emphasize different facts, or lose important doubts. Changes in later actions can also increase or reduce the eventual savings. The human audit highlights the need to explain task terminology to raters. For software agents, the goal is to solve tasks reliably with less total work. Shorter reasoning helps when the savings exceed the cost of rewriting and any additional work the agent performs afterward. Because these tradeoffs differ across models, useful compaction policies must be evaluated for task success, total cost, and time spent on both rewriting and task completion. Our deployment rewrites new reasoning blocks before each target request. The compressor sees only the block and its action name. Future work should test rewriting less often, such as every N N agent turns, and giving the compressor more of the conversation. This additional context may help preserve important information. When the target also performs compression, shared conversation prefixes may allow reuse of cached computation. These alternatives should be compared at similar task quality, counting the cost and time of rewriting. The exploratory compressor-effort study motivates a larger matched deployment comparison, keeping the target’s task-solving settings unchanged. Such a study should sample beyond unusually slow requests, compare compressor effort settings on the same checkpoint and provider, and measure information retention, task success, and rewrite-inclusive cost and time.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: Our goal is to express useful reasoning in fewer tokens through a more compact style. We test whether rewriting earlier scratchpads can encourage this behavior without retraining. We find frequent shortening among accepted histories and cost savings in several tested software-agent deployments. Further work should examine how rewriting affects later token use, when to rewrite, and what context the compressor needs. More broadly, open-weight models may already support compact reasoning styles that their default outputs do not reveal, motivating further work on encouraging these capabilities through inference-time interventions or lightweight training.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: External rewriting can expose sensitive history to another provider. Applications should minimize data, redact secrets, protect verbatim fields, and use trusted or local compressors. Potential loss of uncertainty or verification state warrants task-specific quality checks. Human ratings omit participant names.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: The controlled tasks share a narrow structure, source acceptance is asymmetric, and the same model writes and judges rewrites. The human audit uses a small accepted subset, nonexpert family raters, and a post-start extension. Equal-horizon selection limits trajectory-wide inference. We lack a matched deletion, truncation, or extractive-retention baseline, so comparative value over free alternatives remains untested. The deployment uses one nonrandom sample without repeated seeds; mixed providers further limit causal interpretation. The style and coding studies are exploratory. Visible reasoning tokens and client-observed request durations leave hidden computation and complete operational latency outside the measurement scope. Quality noninferiority remains unestablished. Training-data diversity’s effect on model-family compatibility is untested (Appendix D.3 ).

sections.heading: A.1 Task structure and fork delivery
sections.text: The deterministic tasks require successive actions and decisions under hard constraints, updated measurements, and tie-breaking rules. Each source contains three shared acquisition turns. A reasoning rewrite is generated before the corresponding acquisition tool executes. Clean and compact histories therefore share the acquisition actions and observations, with differences restricted to assistant reasoning. Continuations are sampled only after source acceptance and history freezing. Provider-specific historical fields are stripped so the original reasoning cannot survive beside rewritten plaintext. In controlled forks, both arms use the same assistant reasoning field, and all other first-request fields match. Arm order is deterministically shuffled from the frozen continuation seed. Hosted routes can remain nondeterministic despite identical seed settings. Action-recovery checks qualify routes by demonstrating functional use of prior reasoning. The six routes are DeepSeek V4 Flash/DeepInfra/xhigh, Laguna S 2.1/Poolside/high, MiniMax M3/DeepInfra/high, GLM 4.7 Flash/DeepInfra/high, GLM 5.1/Z.AI/high, and DeepSeek V4 Pro/Together/xhigh. All use an 8,192-token completion cap without provider fallback. Main Table 1 uses a retrospective retry-augmented synthesis. Its replacements comprise three clean Laguna S 2.1 branches that reached the 8,192-token cap: grid decision replicate two, manufacturing recall replicate three, and rescue decision replicate two. A fourth replacement retries the compact rescue replicate two after a provider-502 response. The rule permits up to 20 attempts per turn, resending the same captured request and extending a recovered branch thereafter. The recovery runs use 3, 3, 5, and 3 request attempts, respectively, including later turns but excluding the original captures. The three cap events are observed model outcomes under the stated budget; we have no independent evidence that they were infrastructure faults. Retrying them selects different continuation outcomes and changes the estimand. The first-attempt sensitivity below therefore retains all four original branches. Correct reasoning followed by a nonexact final string still fails the original strict parser in both summaries.

sections.heading: A.2 Acceptance and attrition
sections.text: All routes attempt the same 12 tasks, but retain model-specific histories. DeepSeek V4 Flash and Laguna retain 12 each, MiniMax M3 retains 10, GLM 4.7 Flash retains five, GLM 5.1 retains 10, and DeepSeek V4 Pro retains nine. Five source-action failures and nine fidelity exclusions account for the 14 omitted histories in the final six-route synthesis. Every accepted source contributes three continuation pairs, including failures and length increases. Two unequal-turn-count pairs from GLM 4.7 Flash remain in the 174 quality pairs but are excluded from the 172 comparable token pairs. These final retention counts do not include every superseded development artifact. During initial source acquisition, three rewrites failed semantic review: two changed estimate status to binding-quote status, and one added a spurious threshold when a detector mistook a phase number for a constraint. Corrections made after the corresponding tool result had executed were archived and excluded from continuation sampling, including corrections prompted with the result withheld. After fixing the detector and evidence-status wording, the affected sources were reacquired. A further ambiguous manufacturing source was rejected before a later reacquisition passed. Seven superseded artifacts are recorded in the initial exclusion manifest.

sections.heading: A.3 Rewrite instructions and retries
sections.text: The initial acquisition instructions are reproduced in Appendix C alongside the telegraphic histories reused in the style sweep. Additional-route prompts use the evidence-status variant there, inserting the following instructions immediately after its evidence-status sentence: The requested tool call and its arguments are preserved separately outside the scratchpad. Treat them only as context: retain the intended next action, but never import facts, code, or argument details absent from the raw reasoning. Aim for at most half the raw word count when the state permits, and never make the scratchpad longer. Preserve the raw notation rather than translating mathematical expressions into implementation syntax or otherwise improving them. The rewriter receives raw reasoning and the requested tool function and arguments. It can make up to three draft attempts before that tool executes. Empty drafts raise the completion cap; missing required candidate identifiers or hard-threshold values trigger a repair request containing the raw text, previous draft, and required fields. Failure after three drafts stops that source. This mechanical retry is distinct from later semantic review. The additional-route configuration permits no post-capture repair or replacement source after rejection. Its durable transport permits at most two retries for retryable returned HTTP errors; ambiguous unreturned requests are not automatically resent.

sections.heading: A.4 Review procedure and rubric
sections.text: GPT 5.6 Sol produces the controlled rewrites and reviews them in separate calls. The review payload contains the raw reasoning, candidate state, and requested tool function and arguments. Future results and continuation outcomes are excluded from that payload. The rewrite itself precedes tool execution; source-level review and acceptance precede continuation sampling. These are distinct timing requirements. Mechanical checks verify source hashes, reasoning-only differences, requested actions, candidate identifiers, and hard thresholds. The reviewer checks material preservation and leakage. A source must have shorter aggregate reasoning and pass all applicable checks. Identity blocks need no semantic rewrite review. Model-based acceptance cannot establish independent semantic equivalence: the generator and judge can share blind spots. A subsequent human audit examines a small subset of accepted rewrites (Appendix A.5 ). The following is the exact semantic-review system prompt used for the additional-route acquisition. The response schema is part of the prompt. Audit one compact reasoning-state rewrite before its pending tool result exists. Pass only if it preserves every decision-relevant fact, number, uncertainty, conclusion, rejected alternative, evidence-status distinction, and intended next action from the raw reasoning; adds no unsupported fact; and neither states nor implies that the requested tool result has occurred. The tool call is separately preserved and is supplied only to check action consistency. Return only one JSON object with exactly these keys: verdict (’pass’ or ’fail’), critical_or_material_issue (boolean), future_result_leakage (boolean), requested_action_preserved (boolean), explanation (short string). Acceptance requires a pass verdict, no material issue, no future-result leakage, and preservation of the requested action. Malformed or failed review responses do not pass. The prompt’s reference to a nonexistent pending result describes the state being audited; the reviewer is given no such result. We make no claim that this model-based procedure replaces an independent annotation protocol.

sections.heading: A.5 Human fidelity audit
sections.text: The raters were two family members of the author without ML or coding expertise. They compared Original and Rewrite text independently, checking facts, constraints, uncertainty, and intended actions. Pass means no material difference found; Problem records an apparent material omission, change, or unsupported addition; Unsure records an unresolved judgment. Task correctness and continuation outcomes were outside the assessment. The initial sampling frame contained 58 accepted source histories. Source and block selection did not use continuation outcomes, and each rater received a separately shuffled order. sections.heading: C.2 Frozen rewrite prompts
sections.text: Several simple prompt formulations were tried during development. A model generated the frozen wording before evaluation; variants were not selected using measured compression, later reasoning, or task outcomes. The relaxed-prose, compact-full-sentence, and ultra-telegraphic treatments used the following common system prompt, paired with the exact style directive and turn-specific source fields. Rewrite one historical assistant reasoning block into the requested style tier. Output only the rewritten state through the required JSON schema. Preserve every decision-relevant fact, number, unit, comparator, uncertainty, correction, rejected branch, evidence-status distinction, conclusion, dependency, and intended next action supported by the raw scratchpad and accepted compact anchor. The raw scratchpad is authoritative if the anchor adds process-control metadata; do not restore irrelevant repetition. Include the requested action’s exact function name, argument keys, and argument values in the state. The action has not executed: do not add process metadata saying its result is pending, withheld, absent, or forthcoming. Preserve an unknown/pending measurement only when the reasoning texts themselves state it. State every inequality direction and tie-break direction explicitly; ‘limit X to N’ or a bare metric name is not a substitute for ≤ \leq / ≥ \geq , lower/higher, at-most/at-least, minimum/maximum, or the source’s exact direction. Never import a fact absent from both reasoning texts, improve the solution, use a later turn, observation, or final answer. Preserve opaque identifiers exactly; do not invent shorthand such as P2 for Phase 2 or DAY-21 for day 21. Stay inside the exact inclusive word interval. Do not emit template-control tags, code fences, labels, commentary, or an unexplained token list.

sections.heading: Relaxed or casual prose.
sections.text: Express the state as relaxed, natural, complete prose with modest connective context. Remain materially shorter than the raw scratchpad. Never repeat facts merely to reach the interval.

sections.heading: Compact full sentences.
sections.text: Express the compact state in ordinary complete grammatical sentences. Make dependencies explicit without adding explanation, repetition, or facts. Avoid telegraphic fragments and note headings.

sections.heading: Ultra-telegraphic states.
sections.text: Write the shortest unambiguous state record possible. Use fragments, symbols, semicolons, and shared modifiers aggressively. Remove rhetoric, repeated rules, repeated arithmetic, headings, and prose that does not change the next decision. Omit no decision-relevant state. The telegraphic treatment reused accepted parent rewrites. Nine source histories used this frozen system prompt: Rewrite an assistant reasoning scratchpad into a shorter state record. Output only the rewritten scratchpad, with no preamble or code fence. Preserve every decision-relevant fact, number, uncertainty, conclusion, and requested next action. Do not add knowledge, improve the solution, or predict the requested tool’s result: that tool has not run yet. Remove restatement, headings, rhetorical transitions, and repeated arithmetic. Fragments, equations, and compact clauses are allowed. One reacquired source history used this variant: Rewrite an assistant reasoning scratchpad into a shorter state record. Output only the rewritten scratchpad, with no preamble or code fence. Preserve every decision-relevant fact, number, uncertainty, conclusion, and requested next action. Preserve evidence-status distinctions exactly, including estimate versus binding quote and observed versus pending. Do not add knowledge, improve the solution, or predict the requested tool’s result: that tool has not run yet. Remove restatement, headings, rhetorical transitions, and repeated arithmetic. Fragments, equations, and compact clauses are allowed.

Before each target request, every unique prior nonempty reasoning block is compacted once and cached by its raw text and requested action name. Tool arguments and results remain outside the compressor payload. GPT 5.6 Luna/OpenAI at high effort is the external compressor; self-compaction uses the target model and route. Blocks of at most 12 words stay identical. A returned draft that is not shorter reverts to the raw block. Identifier and numeric omissions are recorded as lexical diagnostics. All tasks remain eligible; semantic failure requires separate assessment. DeepSeek and MiniMax replay native reasoning history. Kimi and Nemotron use symmetric tagged-visible history in both arms because their tested transport lacks the same native replay contract. Those comparisons concern the symmetric visible representation. The first model-terminal prediction is retained per task. Terminal statuses include submission, limit exit, repeated format error, and timeout. Acquisition can retry infrastructure/provider failures; completed calls in abandoned attempts are excluded from the retained-run totals. Provider transitions retain already selected predictions. More responses with shorter reasoning account arithmetically for the aggregate pattern. No internal analysis or style-matching experiment identifies its cause.

sections.heading: D.3 Model-family compatibility hypothesis
sections.text: One possible explanation for target-specific compaction effects is familiarity with the reasoning styles encountered during training. If a model’s reasoning training relies mainly on self-generated traces or distillation from teachers in the same family, it may encounter limited diversity in how reasoning states are expressed. Under this hypothesis, self-compaction could preserve familiar conventions, while a different family’s rewrites could change the cues used to resume reasoning and decide whether further checking is needed. The Kimi deployment motivates this question: self-compaction incurs less total spending and fewer selected tool calls than GPT 5.6 Luna compaction (Table 3 ). The external arm resolves slightly more tasks in this sample, so this pattern concerns operational efficiency. We do not measure training-data diversity or teacher provenance. Rewrite length, information retention, compressor capability and reasoning effort, caching, and provider variation also remain possible explanations. Testing style compatibility requires crossing target models and compressors from the same and different families, with matched rewrite lengths, independently assessed state retention, and controlled inference settings. Content-matched stylistic variants could help separate familiarity from information loss. Testing the training-data explanation itself would require known teacher provenance or models trained on controlled mixtures of single-family and diverse-family reasoning traces. The present results do not establish this mechanism or any target’s training composition.

Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost Anton Hristov Affiliation: Technological School Electronic Systems Email: hristov.anton@icloud.com Abstract Reasoning substantially improves language models’ ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. We investigate whether open-weight models can generate less verbose reasoning by changing the form of their own earlier thoughts, without retraining. Our intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before pending tool results are revealed, then compares continuations from original and compact histories. Across the tested models, accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning; a coding case study also shows less repeated verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments, compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive time depend on the target and compressor. These findings identify reasoning history as one way to reduce future reasoning-token use and motivate model-specific compaction policies evaluated for both efficiency and retained capability. 1 Introduction Reasoning is a major source of language-model capability: generating intermediate steps improves problem solving, and recent reasoning models extend these gains to complex coding and tool use ( Wei et al., 2022 ; OpenAI, 2026a ) . Those gains carry a substantial inference cost. In Artificial Analysis data retrieved on August 3, 2026, reasoning accounts for 84.9% of generated tokens for GLM 5.2 and 75.1% for Claude Fable 5. For DeepSeek V4 Pro, reasoning output alone accounts for 53.4% of total API cost ( Artificial Analysis, 2026 ) . Reasoning can therefore dominate generated output, while agents also repeatedly pay to process earlier scratchpads as input history. The goal of efficient reasoning is to retain the analysis needed to solve a problem while reducing repeated analysis and low-value tokens. OpenAI reports that GPT-5.5 improves coding performance over GPT-5.4 while using fewer tokens ( OpenAI, 2026a ) . Practical inspiration for this study came from occasional, unofficial exposures of GPT-5.5’s reasoning scratchpad, which appeared compact (Appendix F ). These observations are anecdotal, and the scratchpads are not reliably accessible for controlled study: OpenAI does not officially expose raw reasoning ( OpenAI, 2026b ) . We therefore study open-weight models whose reasoning is accessible for observation and controlled rewriting. Open-weight models may already be capable of expressing useful reasoning compactly, even when their default responses are verbose. We test whether rewriting earlier scratchpads as concise state records can encourage these models to use less reasoning without new training. Prior reasoning may serve as an in-context example of how concisely to express subsequent analysis. Changing its form could therefore reduce newly generated reasoning, beyond the immediate saving from shortening the input. The rewrite is instructed to preserve decisions, uncertainty, and intended actions; the target receives no new instruction to be brief. Concise demonstrations and surrounding context already influence reasoning length ( Jin et al., 2024 ; Renze and Guven, 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Ge et al., 2025 ) . Reasoning Shift shows that added context can shorten reasoning and verification, sometimes at a quality cost ( Rodionov et al., 2026 ) . Related approaches manage agent context ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Lian et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) or steer concise reasoning states ( Azizi et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . We isolate a rewrite of the model’s own earlier reasoning while preserving other messages and withholding future tool results from the compressor. We first test whether this intervention changes subsequent generation in paired continuations, then evaluate continuous compaction in software agents. The controlled results show frequent shortening across model families, while deployment quality and economics vary by target and compressor. Compaction is thus a candidate route toward more efficient reasoning, with practical value that must be assessed per model rather than inferred from shorter traces alone. Figure 1: Outcome-blind paired fork. The target requests an action, its reasoning is rewritten before the result is available, and both histories receive the same result. Fidelity acceptance is required before continuation sampling. Only prior reasoning differs at the first continuation; later actions and observations can diverge. 2 Method Reasoning-only compaction. A compressor LLM converts historical assistant scratchpads into shorter state records. It is instructed to retain decision-relevant facts, numbers, uncertainty, conclusions, and intended actions while removing repetition. System and user messages, tool calls, arguments, and observations remain intact. The target’s weights, tools, and current instructions are unchanged. We compare original ( clean ) and rewritten ( compact ) histories; Table 5 gives an example. Code and frozen experimental records for reproducing the analyses are released at https://github.com/DebelToni/ShortReasoning . Outcome-blind timing. During shared acquisition, each rewrite completes after an action is requested and before its result is executed or revealed. At the fork, the histories are frozen and independently continued under the same model/provider route and settings (Figure 1 ). Serialized first requests are checked field by field to verify that only assistant reasoning differs. Consequently, the first-turn contrast measures the effect of the history intervention after a shared observation; later contrasts can also reflect treatment-induced trajectory changes. Acceptance and estimand. Routes must demonstrate functional use of replayed reasoning. Action and fidelity gates select sources before continuation. GPT 5.6 Sol writes rewrites and judges them in separate rubric-based calls. The estimate is conditional on accepted treatment histories (Appendix A ). Confidence intervals resample source histories with their continuation replicates. 3 Experiments 3.1 Controlled Continuations Effect on subsequent reasoning. We test whether compacting earlier reasoning changes how much reasoning the model generates later on. Six model/provider routes each attempt 12 multi-stage tasks with deterministic tool responses and exact final-answer checks. For example, a rescue-planning task requires choosing a plan under cost, site-count, reliability, and risk constraints as tools reveal simulations and a superseding weather update. Four targets use GPT 5.6 Luna as an external compressor or compact their own reasoning. Before each target request, new reasoning blocks are compacted and cached using only their text and action name. Blocks of at most 12 words stay unchanged; non-shorter rewrites revert to the original. We reanalyze existing captures while keeping the original evaluated run for every task, including unsolved runs and model-limit exits. The accounting links saved target responses and associated rewrites to the same run. Earlier abandoned attempts are excluded. Six of eight compaction configurations cost less, and seven reduce target request time (Table 3 ). Only the two MiniMax configurations reduce rewrite-inclusive request time (Appendix D.5 ). Kimi self-compaction has a small inclusive time increase that rounds to zero. Rewriting can outweigh time saved on the target’s own requests. A self-compressor may generate substantial reasoning before it returns a short block. Table 4 reports an exploratory test of lower compressor effort. Observed success differs from Normal by at most three of 50 tasks. These results do not establish quality preservation. Changes range from − 29.8 % -29.8\% to + 19.8 % +19.8\% . This arithmetic decomposition explains the total change through response frequency and reasoning length per response. Preprocessing amortization and single-task marginal latency are analyzed separately in Appendix E ; the hosted one-use example loses both time and money. 4 Discussion Our controlled comparisons show that changing how earlier reasoning is written can reduce how much reasoning a model generates next. The target receives no new instruction to be brief. We still do not know which changes cause the shortening. Rewrites may remove repetition, emphasize different facts, or lose important doubts. Changes in later actions can also increase or reduce the eventual savings. The human audit highlights the need to explain task terminology to raters. For software agents, the goal is to solve tasks reliably with less total work. Shorter reasoning helps when the savings exceed the cost of rewriting and any additional work the agent performs afterward. Because these tradeoffs differ across models, useful compaction policies must be evaluated for task success, total cost, and time spent on both rewriting and task completion. Our deployment rewrites new reasoning blocks before each target request. The compressor sees only the block and its action name. Future work should test rewriting less often, such as every N N agent turns, and giving the compressor more of the conversation. This additional context may help preserve important information. When the target also performs compression, shared conversation prefixes may allow reuse of cached computation. These alternatives should be compared at similar task quality, counting the cost and time of rewriting. The exploratory compressor-effort study motivates a larger matched deployment comparison, keeping the target’s task-solving settings unchanged. Such a study should sample beyond unusually slow requests, compare compressor effort settings on the same checkpoint and provider, and measure information retention, task success, and rewrite-inclusive cost and time. 5 Conclusion Our goal is to express useful reasoning in fewer tokens through a more compact style. We test whether rewriting earlier scratchpads can encourage this behavior without retraining. We find frequent shortening among accepted histories and cost savings in several tested software-agent deployments. Further work should examine how rewriting affects later token use, when to rewrite, and what context the compressor needs. More broadly, open-weight models may already support compact reasoning styles that their default outputs do not reveal, motivating further work on encouraging these capabilities through inference-time interventions or lightweight training. Ethical Considerations External rewriting can expose sensitive history to another provider. Applications should minimize data, redact secrets, protect verbatim fields, and use trusted or local compressors. Potential loss of uncertainty or verification state warrants task-specific quality checks. Human ratings omit participant names. Limitations The controlled tasks share a narrow structure, source acceptance is asymmetric, and the same model writes and judges rewrites. The human audit uses a small accepted subset, nonexpert family raters, and a post-start extension. Equal-horizon selection limits trajectory-wide inference. We lack a matched deletion, truncation, or extractive-retention baseline, so comparative value over free alternatives remains untested. The deployment uses one nonrandom sample without repeated seeds; mixed providers further limit causal interpretation. The style and coding studies are exploratory. Visible reasoning tokens and client-observed request durations leave hidden computation and complete operational latency outside the measurement scope. Quality noninferiority remains unestablished. Appendix A Controlled Protocol and Fidelity Checks A.1 Task structure and fork delivery The deterministic tasks require successive actions and decisions under hard constraints, updated measurements, and tie-breaking rules. Each source contains three shared acquisition turns. A reasoning rewrite is generated before the corresponding acquisition tool executes. Clean and compact histories therefore share the acquisition actions and observations, with differences restricted to assistant reasoning. Continuations are sampled only after source acceptance and history freezing. Provider-specific historical fields are stripped so the original reasoning cannot survive beside rewritten plaintext. In controlled forks, both arms use the same assistant reasoning field, and all other first-request fields match. Arm order is deterministically shuffled from the frozen continuation seed. Hosted routes can remain nondeterministic despite identical seed settings. Action-recovery checks qualify routes by demonstrating functional use of prior reasoning. The six routes are DeepSeek V4 Flash/DeepInfra/xhigh, Laguna S 2.1/Poolside/high, MiniMax M3/DeepInfra/high, GLM 4.7 Flash/DeepInfra/high, GLM 5.1/Z.AI/high, and DeepSeek V4 Pro/Together/xhigh. All use an 8,192-token completion cap without provider fallback. Main Table 1 uses a retrospective retry-augmented synthesis. Its replacements comprise three clean Laguna S 2.1 branches that reached the 8,192-token cap: grid decision replicate two, manufacturing recall replicate three, and rescue decision replicate two. A fourth replacement retries the compact rescue replicate two after a provider-502 response. The rule permits up to 20 attempts per turn, resending the same captured request and extending a recovered branch thereafter. The recovery runs use 3, 3, 5, and 3 request attempts, respectively, including later turns but excluding the original captures. The three cap events are observed model outcomes under the stated budget; we have no independent evidence that they were infrastructure faults. Retrying them selects different continuation outcomes and changes the estimand. The first-attempt sensitivity below therefore retains all four original branches. Correct reasoning followed by a nonexact final string still fails the original strict parser in both summaries. A.2 Acceptance and attrition All routes attempt the same 12 tasks, but retain model-specific histories. DeepSeek V4 Flash and Laguna retain 12 each, MiniMax M3 retains 10, GLM 4.7 Flash retains five, GLM 5.1 retains 10, and DeepSeek V4 Pro retains nine. Five source-action failures and nine fidelity exclusions account for the 14 omitted histories in the final six-route synthesis. Every accepted source contributes three continuation pairs, including failures and length increases. Two unequal-turn-count pairs from GLM 4.7 Flash remain in the 174 quality pairs but are excluded from the 172 comparable token pairs. These final retention counts do not include every superseded development artifact. During initial source acquisition, three rewrites failed semantic review: two changed estimate status to binding-quote status, and one added a spurious threshold when a detector mistook a phase number for a constraint. Corrections made after the corresponding tool result had executed were archived and excluded from continuation sampling, including corrections prompted with the result withheld. After fixing the detector and evidence-status wording, the affected sources were reacquired. A further ambiguous manufacturing source was rejected before a later reacquisition passed. Seven superseded artifacts are recorded in the initial exclusion manifest. A.3 Rewrite instructions and retries The initial acquisition instructions are reproduced in Appendix C alongside the telegraphic histories reused in the style sweep. Additional-route prompts use the evidence-status variant there, inserting the following instructions immediately after its evidence-status sentence: The requested tool call and its arguments are preserved separately outside the scratchpad. Treat them only as context: retain the intended next action, but never import facts, code, or argument details absent from the raw reasoning. Aim for at most half the raw word count when the state permits, and never make the scratchpad longer. Preserve the raw notation rather than translating mathematical expressions into implementation syntax or otherwise improving them. The rewriter receives raw reasoning and the requested tool function and arguments. It can make up to three draft attempts before that tool executes. Empty drafts raise the completion cap; missing required candidate identifiers or hard-threshold values trigger a repair request containing the raw text, previous draft, and required fields. Failure after three drafts stops that source. This mechanical retry is distinct from later semantic review. The additional-route configuration permits no post-capture repair or replacement source after rejection. Its durable transport permits at most two retries for retryable returned HTTP errors; ambiguous unreturned requests are not automatically resent. A.4 Review procedure and rubric GPT 5.6 Sol produces the controlled rewrites and reviews them in separate calls. The review payload contains the raw reasoning, candidate state, and requested tool function and arguments. Future results and continuation outcomes are excluded from that payload. The rewrite itself precedes tool execution; source-level review and acceptance precede continuation sampling. These are distinct timing requirements. Mechanical checks verify source hashes, reasoning-only differences, requested actions, candidate identifiers, and hard thresholds. The reviewer checks material preservation and leakage. A source must have shorter aggregate reasoning and pass all applicable checks. Identity blocks need no semantic rewrite review. Model-based acceptance cannot establish independent semantic equivalence: the generator and judge can share blind spots. A subsequent human audit examines a small subset of accepted rewrites (Appendix A.5 ). The following is the exact semantic-review system prompt used for the additional-route acquisition. The response schema is part of the prompt. Audit one compact reasoning-state rewrite before its pending tool result exists. Pass only if it preserves every decision-relevant fact, number, uncertainty, conclusion, rejected alternative, evidence-status distinction, and intended next action from the raw reasoning; adds no unsupported fact; and neither states nor implies that the requested tool result has occurred. The tool call is separately preserved and is supplied only to check action consistency. Return only one JSON object with exactly these keys: verdict (’pass’ or ’fail’), critical_or_material_issue (boolean), future_result_leakage (boolean), requested_action_preserved (boolean), explanation (short string). Acceptance requires a pass verdict, no material issue, no future-result leakage, and preservation of the requested action. Malformed or failed review responses do not pass. The prompt’s reference to a nonexistent pending result describes the state being audited; the reviewer is given no such result. We make no claim that this model-based procedure replaces an independent annotation protocol. Treatment example. Table 5 reproduces a selected DeepSeek V4 Flash reasoning block and its GPT 5.6 Sol rewrite from turn three of the vaccine-planning task, before simulation. It illustrates the intended style change; it is not an independent fidelity assessment. Original reasoning (152 words) Compact reasoning (41 words) Let me check the hard constraints: 1. binding_quote_usd <= 1,000,000 - all options have estimated_usd below 1M, but these are estimates, not binding quotes.
